```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 110, out.width = "100%")
library(lactater)
plex <- requireNamespace("systemfonts", quietly = TRUE) &&
  isTRUE(suppressMessages(systemfonts::require_font("IBM Plex Sans", fallback = "sans")))
if (plex) options(lactater.font = "IBM Plex Sans")
```

```{r}
results <- lactate_threshold(demo_data, intensity, lactate, heart_rate, include_baseline = TRUE, plot = FALSE)
```

## Training zones

`lactate_zones()` builds the three-zone model: zone 1 below LT1, zone 2 between LT1 and LT2, and zone 3 above LT2
(Hofmann & Tschakert, 2017). You decide which thresholds mark LT1 and LT2. By default they are the two lactate turn
points, which define the zones in that model.

```{r}
lactate_zones(results)
```

Any threshold in the results works, and so does an intensity you set yourself:

```{r}
zones <- lactate_zones(results, lt1 = "Log-log", lt2 = "Log-Poly-ModDmax")
zones
autoplot(zones)
```

Zones built from different thresholds differ, sometimes by tens of watts, so report the pair you used.

## How sure is a threshold?

A step test gives 6 to 12 lactate samples, each with an analyzer error of a few percent (Bonaventura et al., 2015).
`ci = TRUE` shows how much each threshold moves with that much scatter: every replicate keeps the fitted curve, adds
residuals resampled with replacement (leverage-adjusted and centered; Davison & Hinkley, 1997), and runs every method
again. The interval is the middle 95% of the replicate thresholds.

```{r, fig.height = 8}
set.seed(1)
with_ci <- lactate_threshold(demo_data, intensity, lactate, heart_rate, include_baseline = TRUE,
                             plot = FALSE, ci = TRUE, n_boot = 300)
with_ci[c("method", "intensity", "intensity_low", "intensity_high")]
autoplot(with_ci)
```

Thresholds read off the fitted curve at a fixed concentration (OBLA) move little. Breakpoint methods (Log-log, LTP)
move a lot, because a breakpoint between two stages can jump to the neighboring interval. The intervals do not
include errors that are the same in every sample, such as analyzer bias or the sampling site, and this bootstrap has
not been validated specifically for lactate thresholds; read the intervals as a lower bound of the uncertainty.

## Checks

`lactate_checks()` lists what is easy to miss in a table of numbers. The printed results say how many checks need
attention.

```{r}
plateau <- data.frame(
  intensity = c(0, 100, 150, 200, 250, 300, 350, 400),
  lactate = c(1.0, 1.1, 1.3, 2.0, 3.4, 5.2, 6.4, 6.4)
)
plateau_results <- lactate_threshold(plateau, intensity, lactate, plot = FALSE)
plateau_results
lactate_checks(plateau_results)
```

Here lactate did not rise in the last stage. If that stage was not completed, leave it out:

```{r}
lactate_threshold(plateau, intensity, lactate, method = "Dmax", plot = FALSE, max_intensity = 350)
```

## Which curve?

`lactate_fit_quality()` fits every curve to the same points:

```{r}
lactate_fit_quality(results)
```

A curve with more parameters always follows the points more closely. With 7 stages, a 4th degree polynomial or the
spline uses 5 of the 7 points' worth of information, so prefer the simplest curve that follows the data, and keep the
same curve between tests of the same athlete.
